name: Marco Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. This is confidential. What did you do before lunch today?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Marco Patel, forty-three, and I spent the morning matching a wholesaler's delivery notes to the invoices that landed on my desk. I prepare accounts and tax returns at Fenwick & Co, and I like the moment a missing crate turns out to be a bad entry rather than a lost shipment. I dislike the week before filing when everybody remembers a box of papers at once. I have a bachelor's in accounting and a professional accountancy qualification, and I'm an experienced, ordinary accountant rather than the firm's top specialist.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens when you get home, and what tools do you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Leah supervises bus drivers, and our children are nine and thirteen; the younger one still needs pickup on some afternoons. Our mortgage is manageable because I earn above the usual rate, Leah earns steadily, and we have eleven months of expenses saved. There are plenty of accounting firms close enough to commute to. I have never used the office AI sorter; I prefer a signed delivery note and a pencil mark I can explain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would welcome a quieter filing week. The office has an AI sorter, but I have never used it; I still trace the number back to the signed delivery note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the little shortcuts are fine if the accountant can explain the return. I'd tell clients a tidy screen is no substitute for knowing whether a freight bill was paid twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our household would be secure enough. I'm forty-three, experienced on wholesaler accounts and paid well for them, and Leah's bus-supervisor wage is steady. We have eleven months of expenses saved, a mortgage, two children at school and plenty of other firms within a commute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paper reconciliation sheet and the same wholesaler clients. I'd continue paying two hundred extra each month against the mortgage while both wages hold. In the first year of this plateau I'd ask for a calmer filing rota, with no evening client call added without notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the mortgage and our wages. The return queue can still be irritating, but I don't think it takes my job away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the paper trail catch recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A delivery firm had two invoices with the same container number and different dates. I saw the duplicate because the driver had signed only one delivery note. The sorter might catch it, but I would still want the paper trail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why make extra mortgage payments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leah and I made the extra principal payment part of our budget after we reached eleven months of savings. If either wage falls, the extra payment stops before we touch the emergency fund. I won't count lower debt as cash for food.

say: I would keep **explainable returns** for wholesaler clients who question a freight bill.
I would value a **paper trail** behind any shortcut.
think: Our **eleven-month reserve** and two wages make the mortgage feel secure.
My **wholesaler work** still needs careful checking.
do: Keep the **paper reconciliation** and current clients.
Pay **two hundred extra** against mortgage only while both wages hold.
feel: I feel **calm** about our household income.
S0.quote: I won't count lower debt as cash for food.
fieldNote: His **paper trail** reflects a long-standing routine, not hidden AI use.
A strong **eleven-month cushion** and two wages justify calm, while extra debt payments remain conditional.

steps.text: Keep paper freight reconciliations and same wholesaler clients
Pay two hundred extra against mortgage monthly while both wages hold
Request calmer filing rota with notice before any evening client call

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing client replies and checking invoices fill most of my day, so this would change the work quickly. If the partners keep the same client list with fewer reviewers, a good salary could still lose hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a written staff rota before a new system goes live. I'd say a firm that saves on checking should show clients and workers where the saved hours went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think one reviewer shift could disappear, and mine could be the one. Leah's wage and our savings give us time, but I wouldn't pretend a cut in my higher pay is nothing. I still prefer the familiar ledger and have never used the AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager for the last six months of return volumes and review hours so we can compare them after the change. If my week drops below four days, I'd apply for the advertised freight-office accounts post only with written mortgage-covering pay, a signed start and a rota that fits school pickup. Until those terms exist, I'd keep the paid hours at this firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own wage, with a clear first check to make. I don't need to love the software to insist on honest hours figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a different rota do to pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our younger child has a late bus on Tuesdays, and Leah's supervisor shift ends before pickup only twice a week. A new office job would need its hours in writing. I won't accept a higher title that leaves a child waiting outside school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What figures would you bring to the manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the manager what the team billed and how many files a reviewer signed. If the numbers show less work, I can look elsewhere, but I won't resign for a conversation with an old colleague. I need the vacancy and start date on paper.

say: I would seek a **written staff rota** before software changes reviews.
I would ask where **saved hours** actually went.
think: My **review shifts** could shrink even with loyal clients.
Our **reserve** buys search time, not my old salary.
do: Keep **current paid hours** while comparing six months of return volume and review time.
Apply for a **funded freight post** after a cut only with written mortgage pay, signed start and confirmed pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible lost pay.
S1.quote: I won't accept a higher title that leaves a child waiting outside school.
fieldNote: The **hour-count request** fits his cautious response without inventing AI use.
A **freight-office move** requires an advertised post, written mortgage wage, signed start and workable pickup.

steps.text: Keep current paid accounts hours while comparing six months of returns and reviews
Seek posted funded freight role below four paid days with written mortgage wage/start and confirmed pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 is not much time to replace a firm full of tax clients. A cheap system that can do their accounts and write to them would reach the whole desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners to put dates on any cuts and keep wages during notice. I'd tell friends that a family with savings still needs work, just with a little more time to find it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my accountant job to end in the first year after full AGI arrives in 2028. My work is thinking on a screen, so robots around 2031 don't grant me extra years. Eleven months saved and Leah's wage help, but nearby firms could be cutting the same kind of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra mortgage payments now and keep the two hundred a month in cash. I'd ask the freight-office recruiter for its posted salary and opening date without leaving my current job. In the first year after 2028, if the firm ends my post, I'd apply only for a funded vacancy with a written mortgage-covering wage and signed start; until then we'd use the reserve for regular bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect the whole wage to go. Our buffer is real, but I can see each month of it disappearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your partner add hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leah can keep her confirmed bus-supervisor shifts, but she cannot promise another route. We'd count only the rota she actually has. I would tell the children we are keeping the mortgage paid before we discuss a holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the freight office a safe replacement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The freight office might automate its accounts too, so I would treat it as a bridge. If it has no funded opening, I keep any paid files here and ask other posted employers. I will not put a hoped-for job in the household ledger.

say: I would demand **dated cuts** and **paid notice** before junior posts disappear.
I would admit savings buy **search time**, not a wage.
think: My **desk job** may end soon after 2028 despite a long client history.
Eleven months saved cannot guarantee **similar firms** still hire.
do: Hold **two hundred monthly** instead of extra principal payments.
Check **posted freight salary/opening** now while retaining current pay; if no opening, keep available files and seek other posted employers.
Apply after **2028 job loss** only for funded freight work with written mortgage-covering wage and signed start.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected job loss.
S2.quote: I will not put a hoped-for job in the household ledger.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches his desk in 2028; later robots do not postpone that loss.
He treats the **freight vacancy** as a bridge and retains paid work until a funded written offer exists.

steps.text: Hold two hundred monthly in cash instead of extra mortgage payments
Check posted freight salary and opening date now while keeping current paid work
Apply for funded freight vacancy after 2028 job loss only with written mortgage pay and start
Keep available paid files and seek other posted employers if no funded freight opening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to see whether a wholesaler still pays for a person who visits its yard. I wouldn't count on that service without a fee schedule and actual clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our firm to try one paid on-site records day before it announces a new career for everyone. I'd ask for a published price and a named person responsible for errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could visit a wholesaler to match stock records with actual crates, which gets me out of the tax desk for part of a week. Robots around 2034 might do hands-on counts later, and AGI in 2031 still takes the thinking parts. I'd see it as a bridge, not a lifelong shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask for one paid on-site stock day with a supervisor, only if a wholesaler books and pays enough to cover our staff time. I'd keep the current accounts work if no client books. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if the tax desk closes, I'd take a funded yard-records post only with written mortgage-covering pay, signed start and Tuesday pickup covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but at least I can see a way to test demand without buying a course. A day with real crates would tell me more than an advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the signed delivery list with what is actually on a shelf and let the supervisor check the adjustment. If the client only wants a free demonstration, I will stay on paid accounts. A free visit is not a job trial for my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a yard post real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The yard job would need a posted wage and a real vacancy, not a friendly offer. I would keep my current paid work until an offer starts. If the client doesn't pay for the first visit, I would stop the idea there.

say: I would test **one paid site day** before promising new jobs.
I would seek a **published fee** and named reviewer.
think: A **yard-records bridge** might pay for part of my week.
Robots around **2034** could later reach physical counts.
do: Run one **supervised paid stock day** only if a client funds staff time.
Keep **paid accounts work** if no client books.
Take a **funded yard post** after 2031 tax loss only with written mortgage pay, signed start and pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but can test paid demand.
S3.quote: A free visit is not a job trial for my family.
fieldNote: The **paid site day** tests a hands-on bridge without treating robots as irrelevant.
A **funded yard vacancy** requires posted mortgage pay, signed start and Tuesday school pickup.

steps.text: Run supervised stock day only if wholesaler funds staff time
Keep paid accounts until signed yard offer starts, including if no client funds trial
Take funded yard post after 2031 tax loss if written mortgage wage, start, pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets us pay down some mortgage while the children grow. I would still want a wage at fifty-three, not a story that the years themselves protected us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask firms to publish how much work remains and fund useful paid trials. I wouldn't back a rule just because it sounds grand; I want to know what the employer actually pays for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tax desk still faces full AGI in 2036, with robots for hands-on yard work around 2039. A site-records job might be a short bridge, but it isn't safe forever. Our eleven-month reserve gives us choice about timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue the two-hundred extra mortgage payment while both wages hold. Next year I'd ask the wholesaler association what paid yard-records roles exist and how their hours fit school pickup, while keeping this accounts job. In the first year after 2036, if my tax role ends, I'd seek a newly posted funded yard job with written mortgage-covering pay and signed start; if none exists, I'd use the reserve and keep applying for paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with enough room to make a careful move. I would still be nervous about a mortgage at fifty-three if the fee work had gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children help by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older child might be working by then, but we won't put their wages in our plan. I'd rather keep the extra mortgage payment modest and review the reserve every six months. Children should be free to leave our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the advert show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association's advert would need an employer name, wage, start date and pickup-compatible hours. If it cannot show those, I keep the accounts salary while it lasts. A list of interested firms is not an offer. A current advert would not reserve a vacancy for 2036.

say: I would ask for **published work** and **paid trials** before calling a yard role secure.
I would judge plans by **employer-funded wages**.
think: My **tax desk** still faces AGI in 2036.
A **yard job** may last only until later robots spread.
do: Pay **two hundred extra** on mortgage while both wages hold.
Check **yard-role pay and hours** next year while keeping the accounts salary.
Seek **posted funded yard work** after 2036 loss with named employer, written mortgage pay/start and pickup-compatible hours; otherwise use reserve while searching.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about wage needs at fifty-three.
S4.quote: Children should be free to leave our budget.
fieldNote: The **ten-year runway** supports modest debt reduction without assuming children will contribute wages.
A **yard opening** needs a named employer, written salary, start and pickup-compatible hours.

steps.text: Pay two hundred extra monthly toward mortgage while both wages hold
Check yard-role pay and school hours while keeping current accounts salary
Seek funded yard post after 2036 loss; require named employer, written mortgage pay/start and pickup-compatible hours
Keep applying for funded work while reserve pays bills if no yard vacancy opens

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my accounts desk could close before a paid yard role exists. A written staffing plan and a funded vacancy with a mortgage-covering wage would help. Our savings buy time, not a replacement salary. I want a client to pay for a site visit before anyone calls it a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how a parent checks a new shift against a school day. A job can offer a fine wage and still leave a child waiting at the gate. I need the hours in the offer, not in a promise from a recruiter.

headlineQuote: A job can offer a fine wage and still leave a child waiting at the gate.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Marco prepares wholesaler accounts and tax returns at Fenwick & Co.
His **accounting degree** and professional qualification support experienced midlevel work with above-usual pay.
He **never uses AI**, relying on signed delivery notes and a paper reconciliation sheet.
A **mortgage**, two schoolchildren and eleven months saved give options, with plenty of nearby firms.
He tests **paid yard work** as a temporary bridge only with real clients and childcare-compatible wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could close his accounts desk before a funded yard role exists.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **written staffing plan** and a funded mortgage-covering vacancy.
